title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
gist: Together AI and Ollama explain that agentic coding workloads are prefill-dominated and only economical with prefix caching, which harnesses break by mutating early prompt content (timestamps, late tool insertion, reasoning-effort changes) and engines lose via misrouting or eviction; Together counters with cache-aware routing, CPU offload, PagedAttention and disaggregated prefill/decode over RDMA.

insights.claim: Coding-agent workloads have very large input sequence lengths and very small outputs: each step resends the entire conversation (system prompt, tool definitions, files read, commands run) and typically gets back a tool call only a few dozen tokens long.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Inference demand from agents scales with context length, not output tokens; providers optimized for prefill and cache reuse gain cost advantage.
insights.quote: This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads.
insights.locator: Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern

insights.claim: For agentic workloads, model speed effectively means how fast an engine can process a long history of previous turns, because agent turns are dominated by prefill rather than decode, even for reasoning models once sessions reach tens of thousands of tokens.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Benchmark inference providers on time-to-first-token over long cached prompts, not tokens/sec streaming, when evaluating agent infrastructure.
insights.quote: an agent turn is mostly prefill
insights.locator: A normal chat response spends time

insights.claim: Without prefix caching, the compute redone across an agent session grows with the square of session length: 100 equal-sized turns process 5,050 units of prompt uncached versus 100 with caching (idealized).
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Prefix-cache hit rate is a first-order driver of agent inference cost; vendors that sell cached-token discounts capture this economics.
insights.quote: without caching, the work you redo grows with the square of the session length

insights.claim: A prefix cache matches only up to the first differing token, so appending to the prompt is free while changing even one character near the top forces re-processing of the whole session.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Any harness or API feature that mutates early prompt content silently multiplies inference spend.
insights.quote: Changing anything earlier, even a single character, means re-processing everything after it.
insights.locator: The catch is that a prefix cache

insights.claim: Ollama shipped an 'ollama launch' command letting users connect harnesses like Claude Code, Codex and Pi to open models such as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3 while keeping existing workflows.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Open models are being plugged into closed-vendor agent harnesses, lowering switching costs away from proprietary model APIs.

insights.claim: Translation layers between agent harnesses and model APIs are a frequent cause of prefix-cache breakage, unexplained agent behavior and outright harness errors, imposing time and monetary costs.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Integration quality, not just model quality, determines real-world cost/performance of open models in agent stacks.
insights.locator: Connecting a harness to an API might seem easy

insights.claim: Late-loaded tools found via tool search should be appended at the end of the conversation rather than inserted into the tool list near the top, which can force re-processing of hundreds of thousands of tokens; but some models' chat templates error when a tool definition appears mid-conversation.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Model chat-template design (support for mid-conversation tools) becomes a competitive feature for open models in agent use.

insights.claim: Putting turn-varying values such as timestamps, git status or the working directory in the system prompt turns every agent turn into a full re-read; session-specific values like a user's name also prevent new sessions from reusing cached setups across users.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Harness builders should keep system prompts byte-identical across sessions to unlock cross-session cache hits.
insights.quote: The easiest way to wreck the cache is to put something in the system prompt that changes from turn to turn
insights.locator: Things at the top that change

insights.claim: In GLM-5.3-Flash the chat template writes reasoning effort into the first system block, so raising effort mid-session invalidates nearly the whole cache; the authors advise fixing effort at session start or starting a fresh (or compacted) session instead.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Model-level template choices can make common user actions expensive; a hidden cost factor when comparing open models for agents.

insights.claim: Oversized tool outputs are paid for on every subsequent turn, and truncating them without telling the model (e.g. returning lines 1-100 of a 640-line file silently) leads the model to confidently edit code it never saw; a one-line truncation notice fixes it.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Agent reliability failures often stem from harness engineering rather than model capability.
insights.quote: Cutting it without saying so gets you a model confidently editing code it never saw.

insights.claim: Open models such as Kimi K3, GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash are now good at splitting tasks across subagents, but having subagents inherit the full parent history is not strictly better than a brief, because cached prefix still costs attention compute and GPU memory.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Open models are reaching multi-agent orchestration capability; efficient context scoping is a lever on inference cost.
insights.quote: Inheriting sounds strictly better, but it isn't.

insights.claim: Together AI frames an inference engine as a machine for keeping GPUs busy, citing a single GPU's rental cost at around $50k per year while serving hundreds of concurrent users.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: GPU utilization is the core margin lever for inference providers; idle or redundant compute directly hits economics.
insights.quote: A single GPU costs around $50k to rent per year

insights.claim: Cache-aware routing must send each agent turn to the data center and node holding the session's cache, either via a client-supplied key like prompt_cache_key or by hashing prefixes to find the node with the longest match; misrouting forces recomputation and duplicate storage.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Inference providers with sophisticated cache-aware routing can offer materially cheaper agent workloads.
insights.locator: Routing requests for optimal cache hits

insights.claim: Under load-aware routing, a cache miss on an idle node can be a better deal than queuing at an overloaded warm node, so even a perfectly stable prompt does not guarantee a cache hit.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Cache hit rates depend on provider backend quality, not just client discipline.
insights.quote: sometimes the cache miss might be the better deal

insights.claim: Together AI offloads idle agent sessions' KV cache to CPU memory while tools like tests run, and restores it on the next turn, to free GPU memory for active users.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Tiered memory (GPU/CPU) for KV cache is becoming core inference infrastructure, supporting demand for host memory and interconnect.
insights.locator: Keeping the cache alive between turns

insights.claim: Cache memory headroom, not compute, usually limits how many concurrent requests a GPU can serve; engines use PagedAttention and continuous batching to allocate cache in small blocks and fill freed slots immediately.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Memory capacity/bandwidth (HBM) is the binding constraint for agentic inference, favoring memory-rich accelerators.
insights.quote: headroom for cache memory, not compute, is usually what limits how many requests a GPU can serve at once
insights.locator: The upshot for anyone building a harness

insights.claim: Together AI runs prefill and decode on separate clusters — compute-tuned for prefill and memory-bandwidth-tuned for decode — shipping the cache between them over RDMA so long agent prompts don't slow token streaming for others.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Disaggregated serving drives demand for high-bandwidth networking (RDMA) in inference clusters.
insights.locator: Agents also push the prefill/decode split

insights.claim: Agent performance at long horizons requires both sides to cooperate: a stable harness prompt still loses the cache if the engine misroutes a turn, and perfect routing fails if the harness changes the first line every turn.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
insights.so_what: Vertical coordination between harness and inference provider is a moat; watch for bundled harness+inference offerings.
insights.locator: None of that is visible to the person
